subtopic_title: Conversion of fractions to decimals and vice versa
curriculum_objective_text: Convert fractions to decimals and decimal to fraction

record_links.rationale: This record establishes the prerequisite idea that a fraction must be expressed with a power-of-ten denominator before it can be written as a decimal fraction, which prepares the fractions-to-decimals procedure.

record.evidence_quote: To write a fraction as a decimal fraction, the denominator has to be in a grouping of 10, so it needs to be 10; 100; 1,000; or 10,000, and so on. This is because decimal fractions use the base ten number system.
record.content_text: To write a fraction as a decimal fraction, the denominator has to be in a grouping of 10, so it needs to be 10; 100; 1,000; or 10,000, and so on. This is because decimal fractions use the base ten number system.

record_links.rationale: This exposition directly teaches the first conversion method for this AO: convert common fractions with power-of-ten denominators to decimals using place value.

heading_path.h3: Converting common fractions to decimal fractions

record.content_text:
When a common fraction has a denominator that is a power of ten, it is easy to convert it to a decimal fraction. You dealt with the place values of decimal fractions in Chapter 1.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
    \text{units} & \text{.} & \text{tenths} & \text{hundredths} & \text{thousandths} & \text{ten thousandths} \\
    (1) & \text{.} & \left( \frac{1}{10} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{100} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{1,000} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{10,000} \right) \\
    \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

Consider the fraction $\frac{30}{1,000}$. If the denominator is 1,000, the corresponding decimal fraction must have 3 digits after the decimal point. We may write it in a place value table.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
    (1) & \text{.} & \left( \frac{1}{10} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{100} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{1,000} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{10,000} \right) \\
    \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
    \hline
    0 & \text{.} & 0 & 3 & 0 &  \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

The place value table shows that we have zero units, zero tenths, three hundredths and zero thousandths. Remember that we do not write zeros at the end of decimal fraction. This fraction is therefore written as 0.03.

Similarly, the common fraction $\frac{30}{100}$ may be expressed as 0.30, which is written as 0.3. The common fraction $\frac{30}{10}$ may be expressed as 3.0, which is written as 3.

heading_path.h3: Converting common fractions to decimal fractions

record.evidence_quote: When the denominator of a common fraction is not a power of ten, we use division to convert the common fraction to a decimal fraction.
record.content_text: When the denominator of a common fraction is not a power of ten, we use division to convert the common fraction to a decimal fraction.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 4.7: Converting common fractions to decimal fractions

record.answer_text:
Step 1: Divide the denominator into the numerator. If it cannot divide, write a zero.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{r}
0\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5}\\
\end{array}
$$

Step 2: Put a decimal point after the zero and after the numerator.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{r}
0.\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5.}\\
\end{array}
$$

Step 3: Add zeros after the decimal point in the numerator.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{r}
0.\phantom{0000}\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5.0000}\\
\end{array}
$$

The numbers 5; 5.0; 5.00; 5.000; 5.0000 and so on all represent the value 5.

Step 4: Carry on with the division.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{l}
\phantom{00} 0.8\,3\,3\, ...\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5.0\,0\,0\,0}\\
\,\underline{-0}\downarrow\,\downarrow\,\downarrow \,\downarrow \\
\phantom{00} 5\,0 \\
\,\underline{-4\,8} \\
\,\phantom{000} 2\,0  \\
\phantom{00}\underline{-1\,8} \\
\phantom{00000} 2\,0   \\
\;\phantom{000}\underline{-1\,8}  \\
\;\phantom{000000} 2\,0   \\
\end{array}
$$

Step 5: Write down the answer.

The division will carry on forever, because we keep on getting the same remainder. This is called a recurring decimal. We write it with a dot above the digit that repeats.

$$
\therefore \frac{5}{6}=0.8\dot{3}
$$
